title: Real-World 12 and 18-Month Outcomes of Faricimab in Patients Previously Treated for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration
content: Age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is a significant cause of visual impairment globally.1 This single-centre retrospective study evaluated real-world outcomes of faricimab in patients with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) who responded suboptimally to other anti-VEGF treatment. Patients with nAMD who were switched to faricimab between September and December 2022 with a minimum of 12 months’ follow-up were included. Main outcomes were best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), central subfield thickness (CST), and treatment intervals at 12 and 18 months. A total of 136 eyes received at least one intravitreal faricimab injection, of which 71 eyes (62 patients) with sufficient follow-up data were included in the analysis. Median BCVA changed from 68 ETDRS letters (IQR 57-74) to 66 (55-75, p=0.119) at 12 months and 67 (56-73, p=0.009) at 18 months. Median CST changed from 296 µm (IQR 270-339) at baseline to 273 µm (245-313, p=0.0001) at 12 months and 263 µm (240-300, p<0.000) at 18 months. 5.6% of eyes had a dry macula at baseline, compared to 26.8% (p=0.002) and 31.7% (p=0.001) at 12 and 18 months, respectively. Mean treatment interval changed from 5.2 ± 1.6 weeks at baseline, to 7.4 ± 2.8 weeks (p<0.0000) at 12 months, and 7.5 ± 3.1 weeks (p<0.0000) at 18 months. Adverse events included one case of hypertensive anterior uveitis and one post-injection hypotony. Switching to faricimab for nAMD achieved stable vision, improved anatomical outcomes and extended treatment intervals over 18 months.
